catalog_quote: Cemuhi is of particular interest in being one of the very few Oceanic languages with phonemic tone. This sketch is based on Rivierre (1980). ... Cemuhi also distinguishes three register tones: high, mid and low. Contrast is illustrated in the following minimal triplet: /te:/ [high tone] 'heavy' /te:/ [mid tone] 'run against, jostle' /te:/ [low tone] 'to fly' A number of grammatical morphemes have what Rivierre calls a 'neutral' tone: the tone harmonises with that of the preceding syllable. ... Perhaps 95% of words are isotonal, with only a single specification for tone needed for the whole word. However, the remaining 5% have complex tone patterns, and while in some cases this derives from compounding, in others this pattern occurs on monomorphemic words. 1.3 Stress I have not discovered any discussion of stress patterns in Cemuhi.

new_statements.quote: Les variations tonales attestées dans cette langue ne masquent nullement sa similitude avec le cémahi [scanned for cèmuhî], langue à morphologie tonale pauvre et ignorant complètement le phénomène du couplage⁹. [fn. 9:] Mais non dépourvue de traits accentuels démarcatifs : le ton du lexème se réalise de façon privilégiée sur la syllabe initiale et des neutralisations vocaliques et consonantiques sont attestées en syllabe finale. Cf. J.C.R., 2, 1972 et J.C.R., 6, 1976. [p. 430:] alors qu'une évolution interne au système tonal cèmühî a provoqué l'apparition d'un troisième registre bas, le registre bas du pâicî semble la transposition pure et simple sur le plan tonal de faits initialement accentuels.
new_statements.translation: The tonal variations attested in this language [Paicî] in no way mask its similarity to Cèmuhî, a language with a poor tonal morphology and completely without the phenomenon of coupling. [fn. 9:] But not devoid of demarcative accentual traits: the tone of the lexeme is realized preferentially on the initial syllable, and vowel and consonant neutralizations are attested in the final syllable. Cf. Rivierre 1972 and Rivierre 1976 [unpublished grammar of Touho]. [p. 430:] whereas an internal evolution of the Cèmuhî tonal system produced the appearance of a third, low register, the low register of Paicî seems the pure and simple transposition onto the tonal plane of originally accentual facts.

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog holds Cemuhi with an empty rule and there are no existing statements. Rivierre 1978 supplies the type (register-tone language, three levels) and a demarcative initial-syllable prominence statement (fn. 9), so it fills in rather than contradicts the catalog. If the catalog wants a stress-type label, this supports 'tonal; demarcative initial prominence, non-contrastive'.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Cemuhi is a register-tone language (high / mid / plus a later low register that arose from lexemes with an originally rising scheme, pp. 430, 432); word tone is a property of the lexeme. No contrastive word stress is described. The only accentual statement is demarcative: the lexeme's tone is realized preferentially on the INITIAL syllable, and the FINAL syllable shows vowel and consonant neutralizations, i.e. an initial-syllable prominence that marks word boundaries rather than distinguishing words. Cemuhi lacks the prosodic 'coupling' (couplage) that governs accent groups in Xârâcùù and Paicî.
new_statements.exceptions: None for Cemuhi. Detail on the low register: the fall of the final in originally rising (-') lexemes 'n'est pas totalement réalisé en cémihi et certains lexèmes sont indifféremment (‘’) ou (‘‘)' (p. 432), and a stable rising scheme exists as an expressive innovation. The article's own fieldwork and full accent description (initial-mora accent, higher and more intense; two initial moras accented on units of four or more moras; coupling of accent groups) is for Xârâcùù (Canala), not Cemuhi.
new_statements.identity_note: Rivierre's 'cèmuhî' is the language of Touho (centre-north Grande Terre), i.e. Cemuhi cemu1238 (scanned renders the name as cémahi / cémühi / czmühi). The 1978 article's primary description is of Xârâcùù (Canala, informant Guy Tamai from the Thio region, October 1977) with comparisons to Paicî, Cemuhi and the Far South dialects (Dubea, Numee, Île des Pins); Cemuhi facts are cited from Rivierre 1972 and his unpublished 1976 'Grammaire de la langue de Touho (cemühi)', not from new fieldwork in this paper.

audit.reasoning: Quote confirmed verbatim in the held cache of Lynch 2002 pp. 753-754. The classification (tonal / tonal-OR-pitch accent, no stress rule, domain not stated by the source) rests on a 2002 handbook sketch that is a faithful abstract of the sole reference grammar (Rivierre 1980), and the tonal classification is independently corroborated by held material (Lionnet 2022 fn. 9 quoting Rivierre 2001:32 'languages with word tone'; Ferry's 1982 review of Rivierre 1980, downloaded now: 'possède des tons dont le jeu est très finement décrit'; Wikipedia citing Rivierre 1972/1980). Nothing found on the web (no JIPA illustration, no dissertation, no post-Rivierre Cemuhi prosody study; Lionnet's 2022/2023/2025 accent-and-tone work is on Paici/Xaracuu/Drubea-Numee) suggests a stress system that would change the classification. The weakness is only that the stress line is Lynch's second-hand 'no discussion found' rather than Rivierre's ow

sources.note: The first assessment listed this as print only; it is open on archive.org and was already held under the nemi1240 our files. p. 429 + fn. 9 is the only primary statement on Cemuhi accentual properties: tone language with poor tonal morphology, no 'couplage', but demarcative traits (lexeme tone realised preferentially on the initial syllable; final-syllable neutralisations) — the note the record's the primary-stress rule/caution should carry.
